# Draft:History of joint military drills of the People's Republic of China

Given the short- to medium-length of this article, I hesitate to approve this when it could very likely be placed within the History of the People's Liberation Army article, no?Secondarily, the prose/verbiage needs some work; Axe things like "high complexity", "validating", "tentative", "earnest", etv etc  — MWFwiki (talk) 02:25, 18 March 2026 (UTC)}}
----
The '''History of joint military drills of the People's Republic of China''' (PRC) tracks the People's Liberation Army's (PLA) transition from a closed, continental force to an active participant in global military diplomacy. Since its founding in 1949, the PRC has shifted from a total reliance on Soviet tactical training during the 1950s to conducting high-complexity maneuvers across every continent and major maritime corridor. These exercises now serve as a primary vehicle for testing "jointness" between services, validating domestic hardware, and signaling strategic intent to regional and global actors.
Historical Development
Cold War and Isolation (1949–1978)
Early military cooperation focused almost exclusively on the Soviet Union following the 1950 Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship, Alliance and Mutual Assistance. Soviet advisors provided the doctrinal foundation for the PLA, culminating in the 1955 Liaodong Peninsula exercises which practiced coordinated amphibious and land operations. This period of cooperation ended with the Sino-Soviet split. For the next two decades, the PLA reverted to a doctrine of "Self-Reliance," focusing on internal maneuvers and border defense with virtually no international engagement.
Formative Engagement (1979–2012)
The Reform and Opening Up era introduced tentative exchanges with Western and regional militaries. While the 1980s saw limited technical cooperation with the United States, the modern era of drills began in earnest in the early 2000s. The 2002 founding of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) provided a platform for China’s first multilateral drills, focusing on counter-terrorism and the "Three Evils" (terrorism, separatism, and extremism). In 2003, the PLA Navy conducted its first joint maritime exercise with Pakistan, initiating a sustained shift toward "blue water" diplomacy.
Modern Era and Strategic Integration (2013–Present)
Under the leadership of Xi Jinping, joint drills have moved from ceremonial displays to high-intensity combat simulations. The 2015 military reforms reorganized the PLA into Theater Commands, necessitating more complex, inter-service exercises. By 2025, the scope expanded to include "no-limits" strategic integration with Russia and inaugural exercises with EU candidate states and BRICS+ partners.
Drill Typologies and War Games
The PLA categorizes foreign engagements into distinct functional tiers, ranging from tactical training to strategic theater-level war games.
Strategic War Games and Blockade Simulations
Large-scale maneuvers simulate regional contingencies. The Joint Sword (2024) and Justice Mission (2025) series involved the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Rocket Force to rehearse multi-domain blockades and precision strikes near Taiwan and the South China Sea. These exercises frequently test anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) capabilities to deter international intervention.
Functional and Medical Training
* Counter-Terrorism: Series like Peace Mission and Warrior (Pakistan) focus on urban warfare and hostage rescue.
* Military Medical Diplomacy: Exercises like Combined Aid (with Germany) and Peace Rescue (with Vietnam) test mobile field hospital deployment and disaster response.
* Special Operations: Bilateral drills like Golden Dragon (Cambodia) emphasize special forces integration and small-team tactics.

Strategic Impact and International Response
Maneuvers in disputed corridors are often analyzed as coercive tools. Observers from the United States, Japan, and Australia argue that exercises like Joint Sword and Justice Mission normalize a permanent military presence in contested waters and disrupt international shipping routes.
Technically, these drills have narrowed the gap in PLA interoperability and allowed for stress-testing domestic hardware against foreign counterparts. Recent "far seas" operations in the Arctic and Africa demonstrate an increasing capability for long-range power projection, signifying a departure from traditional near-shore defense priorities.
